_comment: DISA Mozilla Firefox STIG-aligned enterprise policy for the secure travel browser.
policies.json is the STIG's prescribed enforcement mechanism (machine-wide, not
user-overridable). Baseline controls: no add-on installation, no telemetry/data
submission, no password manager or form autofill, no sync/accounts, TLS 1.2 floor,
pop-ups blocked, developer tools off, search suggestions off, downloads always
Deliberate deviations from the analyst-kiosk profile, because the threat model here
is a HOSTILE LAN (hotel wifi), not a contained enterprise enclave:
* No WebsiteFilter kiosk allow-list — this browser is for general browsing.
* DNS-over-HTTPS is ENABLED and pinned to Quad9 (the kiosk disables DoH). On an
untrusted network the local DNS resolver is the adversary; DoH takes name
resolution away from it. Fallback stays on so captive-portal login still works.
* HTTPS-Only mode is on — plaintext HTTP on a hostile LAN is readable and
injectable by anyone on the segment. The per-site 'Continue' button remains
* Clipboard events stay enabled — pasting a URL or a password from the host is
normal use here; there is no case data on screen to exfiltrate.

DNSOverHTTPS._comment: Pinned to Quad9. Fallback true = if the DoH endpoint is unreachable (captive portal not yet accepted) Firefox falls back to the container's resolver long enough to reach the portal.

Preferences._comment_hostile_lan: media.peerconnection: WebRTC's STUN/ICE discloses the machine's local and public addresses to any page that asks and can open peer-to-peer flows that bypass the browser's normal request path — on a public LAN that is a discovery and exfil channel, so it is off. browser.cache.disk: cache is RAM-only; with the profile on container tmpfs nothing browser-derived is ever written to a persistent disk. Referer trimming limits what one site learns about browsing on another.
Preferences._comment_downloads: Downloads are permitted but contained: every download prompts (no silent writes) and files land in a fixed directory on the container's tmpfs — which is destroyed when the browser exits. Nothing the browser writes can reach the host filesystem; there are no writable host mounts.
